judgments.proposition: The Trial Court separately found that the plaintiff had successfully proved possession of the suit property, notwithstanding his failure to prove title.
judgments.stage: Trial Court merits decision, as reported by the Supreme Court
judgments.quote: he had succeeded in proving his possession over the suit property
judgments.gap: The underlying trial evidence is not reproduced in sufficient detail for independent verification. The finding establishes possession within the stated reconstruction policy, not ownership.

judgments.proposition: At the Supreme Court merits stage, the plaintiff was affirmatively characterized as being in settled possession of the suit property, despite his failure to prove title.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: application of settled-possession doctrine
judgments.quote: Nevertheless, he has been found to be in settled possession of the property.
judgments.gap: The conclusion that possession was settled is recorded, but the judgment does not provide enough case-specific details to reconstruct independently every contextual consideration underlying that characterization. The cited opposition passages identify limits for transient trespass, not a contrary finding about this plaintiff.

judgments.proposition: Under the rule articulated by the Supreme Court, peaceful and settled possession may be protected against forcible interference even by a rightful owner. A rightful owner confronting a person already in settled possession must pursue lawful proceedings rather than resort to unilateral forcible eviction.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: governing possession-protection doctrine
judgments.quote: If the trespasser is in settled possession of the property belonging to the rightful owner, the rightful owner shall have to take recourse to law;
judgments.gap: Protection depends on the quality of possession and the circumstances of interference. It is not immunity from lawful eviction, a final title determination, or a categorical prohibition on every act of self-protection by an owner. The judgment recognizes reasonable-force exceptions for certain attempted or insufficiently settled trespasses.

judgments.proposition: The Trial Court left the title question open and decided the suit on established possession and attempted interference. The Supreme Court endorsed that separation of issues.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: review of the Trial Court's chosen scope of adjudication
judgments.quote: The Trial Court therefore left the question of title open and proceeded to determine the suit on the basis of possession
judgments.gap: The court's approval concerns the possession-based injunction on the facts found. It does not establish that the Trial Court determined the underlying ownership contest or settled the parties' precise property boundaries.

judgments.proposition: Counsel for the defendant argued that the suit was defective because it relied on title without seeking a declaration of title, and that failure to prove title required dismissal regardless of the plaintiff's possession.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: defendant-appellant's legal submissions
judgments.quote: the suit ought to have been dismissed without regard to the fact that the plaintiff was in possession
judgments.gap: These are recorded arguments, not accepted legal propositions. The judgment rejects their asserted automatic consequence for the possessory injunction in this case.

judgments.proposition: The Court accepted that an injunction protecting established possession need not fail merely because the plaintiff has not obtained a declaration of title. It endorsed the distinction between leaving unclear title for separate determination and deciding whether proved possession deserves protection against invasion or threatened invasion.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: resolution of injunction-maintainability objection
judgments.quote: it is not necessary for the person claiming injunction to prove his title to the suit land.
judgments.gap: The cited formulation from Fakirbhai concerns lawful possession and invasion or threatened invasion by a person having no title. In this case the recorded finding is that the defendant failed to prove title sufficient to evict, not that his title was conclusively nonexistent. The rule does not establish that every injunction suit lacking a declaration is necessarily maintainable regardless of its facts.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court rejected the defendant's reliance on two High Court decisions as requiring dismissal. It distinguished Sri Dasnam Naga Sanyasi as involving discretionary temporary injunction and explained that Kallappa Rama Londa supported the maintainability of an injunction-only suit without a title declaration.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: treatment of opposing authorities
judgments.quote: upheld the maintainability of a suit merely seeking injunction, without declaration of title
judgments.gap: The supplied judgment summarizes these earlier authorities; their complete decisions are not supplied. The comparison therefore supports only the Supreme Court's reported interpretation, including the distinction between discretionary ad-interim relief and the present merits decree.

judgments.proposition: Whether the plaintiff actually owned the suit land remains unresolved. His assertion of ownership was recorded, but he failed to establish title in the proceeding, and the Supreme Court did not conclusively adjudicate it.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: ownership expressly reserved for other proceedings
judgments.quote: The High Court has kept the question of title open.
judgments.gap: No conclusive ownership adjudication or sufficient underlying title evidence is supplied. Failure of proof does not establish factual absence of ownership; possession and its associated rebuttable presumption also do not establish conclusive ownership.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court expressly clarified that the judgment under appeal must not be understood to have decided ownership of the suit property in favor of or against either party.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: explicit reservation of title and limitation of the judgment's effect
judgments.quote: the impugned judgment shall not be taken to have decided the question of title to the suit property for or against any of the contending parties.
judgments.gap: The reservation leaves the respective ownership claims and their supporting evidence for duly constituted proceedings. No further inference about who ultimately owns the property is supported.

judgments.proposition: Whether the defendant actually owned the suit land or possessed a superior proprietary right remains unresolved. The defendant asserted ownership but did not prove title sufficient to justify evicting the plaintiff in this proceeding.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: ownership expressly reserved for other proceedings
judgments.quote: Each of the two contending parties would be at liberty to plead all relevant facts directed towards establishing their titles
judgments.gap: The judgment does not supply a conclusive determination of the defendant's actual title or the comparative validity of the parties' competing title claims. The defendant's failure to prove better title in this action cannot be converted into a finding that he could never prove it.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court expressly preserved the defendant's ability to bring a separate title-based proceeding and obtain eviction if he establishes a superior legal right to possess the disputed property.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal: express limitation on possessory relief and preservation of proprietary proceedings
judgments.quote: evict the latter on the former establishing his better right to possess the property.
judgments.gap: The availability of a future action is not a prediction that the defendant will succeed. No superior title, entitlement to eviction, or outcome of a later proceeding is established. The possibility of lawful eviction is compatible with protection against immediate unlawful interference.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court found that the appellants' ownership claim lacked concrete evidence and that historical assertions concerning the saint, mosque construction and possession by descendants could not substitute for admissible evidence establishing ownership, possession and title.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, competing title assessment
judgments.quote: Pertaining to the ownership claim of Appellants over the suit property there is no concrete evidence on record.
judgments.gap: Failure to substantiate claimed historical ownership does not establish that every historical event alleged by the appellants was factually false. The relevant conclusion is failure of proof of title on this record.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court reported that Exhibit P1, a copy of the Register of Ancient Protected Monuments, identified the suit property and referred to the Government as owner.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, account of documentary evidence
judgments.quote: the suit property is mentioned and the Government is referred to as the owner
judgments.gap: The document is described within the judgment. Its original pages, precise entries and underlying acquisition instruments are not independently supplied.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court reported that relevant extracts of Exhibit P2, the CTS records, supported the Government's case by showing the property standing in the respondent's name.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, account of documentary evidence
judgments.quote: It shows that the property stands in the name of Respondent.
judgments.gap: The exact CTS extracts are not independently supplied. The judgment treats them as corroboration of the Government's title case rather than as an isolated, self-sufficient title instrument.

judgments.proposition: Syed Abdul Nabi, identified as power-of-attorney holder of original-suit defendants 2A and 2B, testified that the property had been declared a protected monument, displayed a signboard, was possessed by the Government, and contained a building constructed at Government expense.
judgments.stage: Original suit testimony, reported in Supreme Court merits appeal
judgments.quote: He also deposed that the Government is in possession of the suit property
judgments.gap: This records reported testimony, not independent inspection of the property or the witness transcript. The Supreme Court evaluated the testimony together with the documents.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court considered the acquisition manner unchallenged and treated the protected-monuments register entry as valid proof supporting the Government's acquisition case, while observing that possession could have been gained either by acquisition or by assuming guardianship under section 4 of the 1904 Act.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, evaluation of statutory title evidence
judgments.quote: Gaining of possession could be either by acquisition or by assuming guardianship
judgments.gap: The passage does not conclusively isolate which of the two mentioned possession mechanisms occurred. The judgment nevertheless accepts the evidentiary basis for the Government's title in this litigation.

judgments.proposition: On a joint evaluation of Exhibits P1 and P2 and Syed Abdul Nabi's testimony, the Supreme Court concluded that the Government possessed valid title, absolute ownership and continuous possession of the suit property for approximately one century, and that the property was governmental rather than Wakf property.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, title determination
judgments.quote: Their title is valid. The suit property is government property and not of a Wakf character.
judgments.gap: This is the Supreme Court's substantive title finding for the litigated properties. The finding does not mean that possession for approximately one century independently satisfied adverse possession. The title and adverse-possession analyses remain distinct.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court stated that a claimant relying on adverse possession must clearly plead and establish the necessary facts, including when possession began, its nature, the other party's knowledge, its duration, and its open and undisturbed character. The burden rests on the claimant seeking to defeat the true owner's rights.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, adverse-possession pleading and proof requirements
judgments.quote: it is for him to clearly plead and establish all facts necessary to establish his adverse possession
judgments.gap: The specific matters listed by the Court guide pleading and proof, but the judgment does not supply a mechanical aggregation formula for deciding all adverse-possession disputes. The substantive hostile-possession requirement remains independently important.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court found that the Government had not specifically pleaded and proved possession excluding the Wakf appellant with the necessary intention to possess adversely. It also identified deficiencies concerning an earlier title of the appellant and the relevant point of time of disposition.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, application of adverse-possession pleading and proof requirements
judgments.quote: The element of Respondent's possession of the suit property to the exclusion of the Appellant with the animus to possess it is not specifically pleaded and proved.
judgments.gap: The court identifies lack of specific pleading and proof, not a factual finding that every potentially hostile act was impossible or never occurred. The judgment uses the term 'disposition'; this reconstruction does not silently replace it with an independently proved historical dispossession event.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court stated that an adverse-possession plea inherently recognizes title in another person. A claimant's own-title theory and adverse-possession theory are mutually inconsistent in the stated sense that the latter does not begin to operate until the former is renounced and independent hostile possession is asserted and proved.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, relationship between title and adverse possession
judgments.quote: The pleas on title and adverse possession are mutually inconsistent and the latter does not begin to operate until the former is renounced.
judgments.gap: The judgment does not establish a universal procedural prohibition on mentioning alternative pleas in every case. Its operative concern is that an adverse-possession theory must have an independently established basis of hostile possession against another owner, rather than rely on the claimant's asserted lawful title.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court found that the Government had not specifically pleaded and proved possession excluding the Wakf appellant with the necessary intention to possess adversely. It also identified deficiencies concerning an earlier title of the appellant and the relevant point of time of disposition.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, application of adverse-possession pleading and proof requirements
judgments.quote: The element of Respondent's possession of the suit property to the exclusion of the Appellant with the animus to possess it is not specifically pleaded and proved.
judgments.gap: The court identifies lack of specific pleading and proof, not a factual finding that every potentially hostile act was impossible or never occurred. The judgment uses the term 'disposition'; this reconstruction does not silently replace it with an independently proved historical dispossession event.

judgments.proposition: The actual historical occurrence and commencement date of possession by the Government that was hostile to an identified earlier Wakf owner are not affirmatively established by the supplied judgment.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, unresolved historical facts underlying alternative adverse possession
judgments.quote: So are the aspects of earlier title of Appellant or the point of time of disposition.
judgments.gap: The judgment rejects the sufficiency of the adverse-possession case without establishing a positive alternative chronology of hostile entry and dispossession. The inability to prove the necessary facts is not equivalent to proof that the alleged historical circumstances were false.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court concluded that the Government's alternative adverse-possession plea was unsustainable and that the High Court should not have granted support on that ground, even though the Supreme Court independently accepted the Government's title under the Ancient Monuments Act.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, adverse-possession evaluation
judgments.quote: Consequently, the alternative plea of adverse possession by Respondent is unsustainable.
judgments.gap: This is the Court's conclusion on the alternative basis, not a general rule to be assumed before assessing the pleading and proof deficiencies. It does not negate the separately sustained statutory-title finding.

judgments.proposition: On a joint evaluation of Exhibits P1 and P2 and Syed Abdul Nabi's testimony, the Supreme Court concluded that the Government possessed valid title, absolute ownership and continuous possession of the suit property for approximately one century, and that the property was governmental rather than Wakf property.

judgments.gap: This is the Supreme Court's substantive title finding for the litigated properties. The finding does not mean that possession for approximately one century independently satisfied adverse possession. The title and adverse-possession analyses remain distinct.

It also identified deficiencies concerning an earlier title of the appellant and the relevant point of time of disposition.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, application of adverse-possession pleading and proof requirements
judgments.quote: The element of Respondent's possession of the suit property to the exclusion of the Appellant with the animus to possess it is not specifically pleaded and proved.
judgments.gap: The court identifies lack of specific pleading and proof, not a factual finding that every potentially hostile act was impossible or never occurred. The judgment uses the term 'disposition'; this reconstruction does not silently replace it with an independently proved historical dispossession event.

judgments.stage: Supreme Court merits appeal, adverse-possession evaluation
judgments.quote: Consequently, the alternative plea of adverse possession by Respondent is unsustainable.
judgments.gap: This is the Court's conclusion on the alternative basis, not a general rule to be assumed before assessing the pleading and proof deficiencies. It does not negate the separately sustained statutory-title finding.

judgments.proposition: On reading the plaint as a whole, the Supreme Court identified the main controversy as the continuance, term, and duration of the plaintiffs' asserted tenancy of the trust properties, a controversy essentially separate from the requested inquiry into the trust's affairs.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: substantive characterization of the plaint for jurisdictional review
judgments.quote: the main dispute relates to the question of continuance of tenancy and the period of tenancy.
judgments.gap: Identifying the subject of the dispute does not confirm that the plaintiffs' tenancy legally continued, that the asserted eleven-year term was genuine, or that eviction was unlawful.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court distinguished the relief concerning inquiry into trust affairs from the civil claims concerning tenancy. It indicated that, apart from paragraph D of the plaint, the other requested reliefs were of a kind that could be claimed before and considered by civil courts, and that Sections 50 and 51 did not bar civil consideration of the tenancy dispute.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: subject-matter allocation between civil court and trust authorities
judgments.quote: The question of tenancy cannot be decided under Section 50 of the Act.
judgments.gap: Civil court competence to consider a claim is not an award of the claim. The broader language regarding reliefs other than paragraph D must be read alongside the judgment's narrower express direction restricting actual adjudication to tenancy, its terms, and its period. The judgment does not separately develop a comprehensive interpretation of Section 80 beyond the reported objections and its conclusion respecting the tenancy dispute.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court concluded that Sections 50 and 51 did not apply to the component of the litigation concerning tenancy, its terms, and its duration. This supplied the principal jurisdictional reason why wholesale rejection of the plaint could not be sustained.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: application of public-trust statutory provisions to the identified principal dispute
judgments.quote: Sections 50 and 51 of the Act would not have any application to that part of the relief which relates to question of tenancy, the term of tenancy and the period of tenancy.
judgments.gap: This is a legal characterization of the subject-matter jurisdiction, not proof of the asserted tenancy. It does not remove the consent requirement for trust-affairs relief or decide all possible statutory, procedural, or evidentiary objections to individual remedies.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court treated inquiries into the affairs of the public trust as falling under Section 50 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act and recognized the requirement of prior Charity Commissioner consent under Section 51 for suits of the kind specified in Section 50. It accepted the trust's objection to that extent.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: statutory exception concerning trust-affairs relief
judgments.quote: To that extent Mr. Savant is right that the reliefs relatable to Section 50 would require a prior consent in terms of Section 51.
judgments.gap: The statutory exception must not be omitted or generalized into a bar of the tenancy dispute. The judgment does not establish that the requisite consent was obtained or that trust-affairs inquiries could proceed without it. The Charity Commissioner identified in the consent requirement must not automatically be treated as identical to the Assistant Charity Commissioner named as a defendant.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court stated that Section 51 applies to suits by persons having an interest in the trust and that a tenant of a trust does not fall within that statutory category merely by being its tenant.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: statutory interpretation distinguishing tenancy from trust interest
judgments.quote: A tenant of the trust does not fall within the category of a person having an interest in the trust.
judgments.gap: This proposition describes the legal treatment of a trust tenant; it is not independent proof that these particular plaintiffs possessed an existing or continuing tenancy. No general definition covering all other potential categories of trust interest is supplied.

judgments.proposition: Order VII Rule 11 does not authorize rejecting only a portion of a plaint. Order VI Rule 16 separately provides for striking out or amending objectionable pleading matter. Accordingly, a court cannot justify wholesale rejection merely by identifying problems with some distinct pleaded matters or requested remedies.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: distinction between rejection and striking out pleadings
judgments.quote: Order VII Rule 11 does not justify rejection of any particular portion of the plaint.
judgments.gap: The restriction on partial rejection does not mean every requested remedy must ultimately survive or be granted. The distinct procedures for relinquishment, amendment, striking out, and merits adjudication must remain separate.

judgments.proposition: Order II Rules 1 and 2 require a plaintiff to frame a suit to address the whole claim arising from the cause of action and restrict later litigation concerning intentionally omitted or relinquished portions. The Supreme Court indicated that any proposed relinquishment of reliefs should be pursued through an appropriate application before the trial court.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: treatment of combined claims and proposed relinquishment
judgments.quote: If the plaintiffs as contended by Mr. Mohta want to relinquish some reliefs prayer in that regard shall be done before the trial Court.
judgments.gap: The judgment does not establish that a relinquishment application was subsequently filed or granted. It also does not determine the future preclusive consequences of any actual relinquishment. The cited rules cannot be converted into an automatic procedural cure without the required application.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court distinguished the relief concerning inquiry into trust affairs from the civil claims concerning tenancy. It indicated that, apart from paragraph D of the plaint, the other requested reliefs were of a kind that could be claimed before and considered by civil courts, and that Sections 50 and 51 did not bar civil consideration of the tenancy dispute.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: subject-matter allocation between civil court and trust authorities
judgments.quote: The question of tenancy cannot be decided under Section 50 of the Act.
judgments.gap: Civil court competence to consider a claim is not an award of the claim. The broader language regarding reliefs other than paragraph D must be read alongside the judgment's narrower express direction restricting actual adjudication to tenancy, its terms, and its period. The judgment does not separately develop a comprehensive interpretation of Section 80 beyond the reported objections and its conclusion respecting the tenancy dispute.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court's operative limitation confined the contemplated civil adjudication to the question of tenancy, its terms, and its period, while allowing an opportunity to seek lawful relinquishment of remaining reliefs. This records the scope of the procedural outcome rather than supplying an independent premise about the merits.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: operative direction concerning the continued suit
judgments.quote: the adjudication in the suit would be restricted to the question of tenancy, terms of tenancy and the period of tenancy only.
judgments.gap: This is a comparison-only disposition record, not an antecedent proving that the plaint must survive. No subsequent trial, amendment, relinquishment application, or final tenancy finding appears in the supplied judgment. The scope direction must not be expanded into an adjudication of every originally requested remedy.

judgments.proposition: The plaintiffs alleged that they had been forcibly dispossessed despite the continuance of their tenancy and advanced an argument that a person in settled possession could obtain protection against dispossession otherwise than through due process.
judgments.stage: Plaintiffs' pleadings and appellate submissions
judgments.quote: The plaintiffs were dispossessed illegally and a person dispossessed illegally was entitled to protection.
judgments.gap: TRUE records that the plaintiffs made the allegation and legal submission. It does not establish actual forcible dispossession, settled possession, absence of consent, or dispossession without due process.

judgments.proposition: The defendant trust disputed forcible dispossession, contended that possession had been taken lawfully or surrendered voluntarily by tenants, and challenged the plaintiffs' conduct and entitlement to relief.
judgments.stage: Defendant trust's submissions in appellate proceedings
judgments.quote: There was no forcible dispossession as claimed.
judgments.gap: TRUE establishes the trust's opposing position, not the lawfulness of its conduct. The judgment does not resolve whether the disputed possession was surrendered voluntarily, recovered under legal process, or taken forcibly.

judgments.proposition: Whether the plaintiffs were actually dispossessed forcibly, without consent, or otherwise than in accordance with law remained contested. The plaintiffs alleged illegality while the trust asserted lawful recovery and voluntary surrender; the Supreme Court did not resolve the factual conflict.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court review: unresolved merits issue reserved for potentially relevant trial consideration
judgments.quote: This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust
judgments.gap: The competing positions are reported but not factually reconciled. The judgment provides no conclusive finding on the mechanism or timing of dispossession, consent, legal process, the precise possession of individual plaintiffs, or operation of the trial court's injunction during the relevant period. CONFLICTED reflects substantive opposition, not a judicial finding that either version is false.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court's operative limitation confined the contemplated civil adjudication to the question of tenancy, its terms, and its period, while allowing an opportunity to seek lawful relinquishment of remaining reliefs. This records the scope of the procedural outcome rather than supplying an independent premise about the merits.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: operative direction concerning the continued suit
judgments.quote: the adjudication in the suit would be restricted to the question of tenancy, terms of tenancy and the period of tenancy only.
judgments.gap: This is a comparison-only disposition record, not an antecedent proving that the plaint must survive. No subsequent trial, amendment, relinquishment application, or final tenancy finding appears in the supplied judgment. The scope direction must not be expanded into an adjudication of every originally requested remedy.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court separately recognized that entitlement to an injunction is governed by discretionary equitable principles and cannot be inferred automatically from a possible right to recover possession under Section 6. It discussed the principle that a person in unlawful possession cannot obtain an injunction against the true owner to perpetuate that wrongful possession.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: separate substantive principles governing injunctions
judgments.quote: It is settled law that no injunction could be granted against the owner at the instance of a person in unlawful possession.
judgments.gap: The distinction requires a substantive assessment of possession, ownership, conduct, the nature of requested protection, and applicable injunction principles. The Supreme Court did not find that these plaintiffs were trespassers in unlawful possession or determine that the defendant trust had proved every element necessary to defeat an injunction. The legal standards are not an automatic checklist deciding the case.

judgments.proposition: Whether the plaintiffs were actually dispossessed forcibly, without consent, or otherwise than in accordance with law remained contested. The plaintiffs alleged illegality while the trust asserted lawful recovery and voluntary surrender; the Supreme Court did not resolve the factual conflict.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court review: unresolved merits issue reserved for potentially relevant trial consideration
judgments.quote: This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust
judgments.gap: The competing positions are reported but not factually reconciled. The judgment provides no conclusive finding on the mechanism or timing of dispossession, consent, legal process, the precise possession of individual plaintiffs, or operation of the trial court's injunction during the relevant period. CONFLICTED reflects substantive opposition, not a judicial finding that either version is false.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court expressly left the forcible-dispossession plea for possible consideration before the trial court. If raised, that court was to evaluate its relevance and accept or reject the plea according to law; the Supreme Court declined to express an opinion on its merits.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court: express reservation of the contested dispossession issue
judgments.quote: We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.
judgments.gap: The reservation is not an affirmative factual finding of forcible dispossession and not a declaration of entitlement to an injunction or restoration. The trial court's consideration is expressly conditioned on the plea being raised and its relevance to the suit, and must be understood alongside the restriction of the continued adjudication to tenancy questions.
